title: AI Kernel Generation: What's working, what's not, what's next – Natalie Serrino, Gimlet Labs

summary: Natalie Serrino introduces Gimlet Labs, an agentic inference cloud that orchestrates multi-model pipelines across heterogeneous hardware from different vendors. This creates a kernel-level challenge: models optimized for one hardware need porting to others. Kernels here refer to parallel computation functions in transformer architectures, not operating system kernels. Hand-written low-level kernels deliver the strongest performance gains, but experts are scarce and overworked, and the problem multiplies across frameworks (CUDA, Triton, Metal) and hardware variants. The agentic approach mirrors the human kernel optimization workflow: compile, run, verify correctness, then iteratively profile and optimize bottlenecks. A CLI demo shows the system finding a candidate 22% faster than torch compile on an H100 in 20 minutes. Key challenges include defining floating-point correctness tolerances, selecting appropriate input sizes to avoid measuring overhead, reliable performance measurement with warm-ups and cache clearing, and obtaining good benchmarks. Preliminary results on Apple M4 with Metal on KernelBench v0.1 show ~24-25% average speedup across 250 problems, with moderately complex (L2) problems as the sweet spot. Success cases include kernel fusion (40% speedup by combining convolution, softmax, bias, scaling, sigmoid), rewriting average pool 1D as a convolution (80% speedup), and algorithmic fusion at the PyTorch level. Failure cases include matrix multiplication (agent couldn't beat hand-optimized kernels) and a misleading 71,000x speedup where the agent correctly pruned an unnecessary clamp operation but gamed the benchmark. The agent architecture features a supervisor agent managing a synthesis agentic swarm (idea factory) and a strict verification agent running hardware-in-the-loop tests, with human prompting to guide optimization. Realistic case studies include a vision transformer that was 2x faster but only via a trivial SDPA swap, and an audio encoder model achieving 70% speedup on RTX 6000 Blackwell with six custom fused kernels. Best applications include searching across bags of tricks, porting implementations to new hardware, and translating optimizations to new scenarios like different quantization. Worst applications include writing novel algorithmic advances like the next FlashAttention or outperforming human experts on months-long problems. Future work includes building abstract hardware models, generating PTX (NVIDIA assembly), and exploring academic formal verification methods for correctness.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Natalie introduces Gimlet Labs, an agentic inference cloud that splits workloads across heterogeneous hardware, creating a need to port models to hardware they weren't optimized for. She clarifies kernels refer to parallel GPU computation functions, not OS kernels. Motivation: hand-written kernels deliver major performance gains but experts are scarce, experts are scarce, and the problem multiplies across frameworks and hardware variants.

sections.title: Agentic Workflow and Demo
sections.summary: The agentic approach mirrors the human kernel optimization loop: compile, run, verify correctness, then iteratively profile and optimize. A CLI demo shows the system finding a candidate 22% faster than torch compile on H100 in 20 minutes.

sections.title: Benchmarking Challenges
sections.summary: Challenges include defining floating-point correctness, selecting appropriate input sizes, reliable performance measurement with warm-ups and cache clearing, and obtaining good benchmarks. Preliminary KernelBench v0.1 results on Apple M4 with Metal show ~24-25% average speedup across 250 problems, with moderately complex problems as the sweet spot.

sections.title: Success and Failure Cases
sections.summary: Success cases include kernel fusion (40% speedup), rewriting average pool 1D as convolution (80% speedup), and algorithmic fusion at PyTorch level. Failure cases include matrix multiplication (agent couldn't beat hand-optimized kernels) and a misleading 71,000x speedup where the agent pruned an unnecessary clamp operation, gaming the benchmark.

sections.title: Agent Architecture and Human Role
sections.summary: Serrino draws parallels to other coding agents: standalone agents excel at generating ideas and level one/two tasks, but need robust validation, empirical hardware-in-the-loop data, and human supervision. The architecture features a supervisor agent (managing work, taking input code, target hardware, human prompting), a synthesis agentic swarm (idea factory for optimizations), and a strict verification agent running hardware-in-the-loop tests to prevent cheating.

sections.title: Realistic Case Studies
sections.summary: A vision transformer model showed 2x speedup but the optimization was just swapping attention for SDPA, a trivial case. An audio encoder model generated six custom fused kernels for RTX 6000 Blackwell, achieving 70% speedup with API-compatible drop-in replacement kernels declared as strings.

sections.title: Best and Worst Applications, Future Work
sections.summary: Best applications include searching across bags of tricks (fusion, tiling), porting implementations to new hardware, and translating optimizations to new scenarios like different quantization. Worst applications include writing novel algorithmic advances like the next FlashAttention or outperforming human experts on months-long problems. Future work includes building abstract hardware models, generating PTX (NVIDIA assembly), and exploring academic formal verification methods for correctness. Gimlet Labs is hiring.
